questions.title: How can an expert's 'confusing' or 'self-contradictory' testimony ever constitute substantial evidence to survive a JMOL motion?
questions.question_body: In the '134 patent section, the court reverses the jury's infringement verdict because Dr. Wells gave inconsistent testimony regarding whether the 'modeled PIM path' or the variables 'x1/x2' constituted the 'interference generating signals.' He initially mapped them one way, then pivoted without clarifying, leading the court to say his testimony wasn't clear enough. My confusion is about the evidentiary standard: If I understand correctly, at JMOL we view evidence in the light most favorable to the verdict. How does a judge decide that an expert's ambiguity means *no* reasonable jury could find infringement, rather than just weighing conflicting expert opinions? Is there a threshold where contradiction equals total lack of evidence?

questions.title: Does amending a patent claim from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals' always constitute a disclaimer of scope for devices using only two unique inputs?
questions.question_body: Regarding the '775 patent, Finesse amended their claims during prosecution to specify 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' instead of 'two or three,' apparently to distinguish from prior art that used two inputs. However, the Federal Circuit held this didn't amount to a 'clear and unambiguous disavowal' of scope for products using only two unique input signals (like x1 and x2), provided they were 'separately identifiable.' Why isn't adding a specific number ('three') usually interpreted as excluding anything less? What distinguishes this case from typical prosecution history estoppel scenarios where narrowing amendments restrict claim scope?

questions.title: Can an appellate court consider new mappings or theories of infringement raised for the first time on appeal when overturning a jury verdict?
questions.question_body: On appeal regarding the '775 patent, Finesse tried to explain how their expert's identification of three distinct multiplications mapped onto the seven claimed multiplications by citing new arguments and interpretations of Nokia documents that weren't fully developed at trial. The court explicitly stated that Finesse attempted to clarify this mapping on appeal but noted that this evidence was never presented to the jury. Since JMOL is reviewed based on whether *substantial evidence* existed at trial, why does it matter if Finesse offers a better theoretical explanation later? Does raising new theories on appeal automatically invalidate a jury verdict even if some thread of logic existed at trial?

questions.title: What is the precise relationship between reviewing JMOL denials under regional circuit law versus federal patent law standards?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that for non-infringement JMOL denials, they review under Fifth Circuit law (de novo), looking for evidence pointing so strongly one way that no reasonable juror could disagree. Yet they also mention reviewing factual findings for infringement for 'substantial evidence.' Are these actually different standards in practice? How does the Federal Circuit reconcile its own precedent (which often emphasizes claim construction de novo) with the requirement to defer heavily to state/circuit jury verdicts when applying local civil procedure rules like Rule 50?

questions.title: If infringement is reversed via JMOL due to lack of substantial evidence, does that automatically mandate vacatur of damages regardless of how strong the damages theory was?
questions.question_body: The court reverses both patents on non-infringement grounds and consequently vacates the entire $166M damages award. I want to confirm my understanding: Even though Appellants also appealed specifically on damages/new trial grounds (arguing perhaps there was no valid royalty base), did they need to win those separate arguments? Or does establishing non-infringement via JMOL act as a complete bar to recovery immediately upon reversal? Is it procedurally possible for a court to affirm non-infringement but remand solely on damages if there was some other theory of liability not addressed by JMOL?
